claims.text: Lattice strain governs ethanol oxidation performance in Pt-based nanoscale catalysts.
Lattice strain shifts the Pt d-band center.
Shifts in the Pt d-band center modulate the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates such as CH3CO.
Strain-mediated changes in intermediate adsorption enhance ethanol-oxidation kinetics.
Strain-mediated changes in intermediate adsorption enhance catalyst durability.
The as-synthesized Pt-based nanoscale catalysts possess an inherent lattice-strain state.
Vacuum annealing at 300–400°C can induce or relax lattice strain in the Pt-based catalysts.
Lattice strain changes the surface atomic arrangement of Pt.
Thermal annealing alters lattice strain, which subsequently shifts the Pt d-band center.
A maintained strain state stabilizes reaction intermediates involved in complete ethanol oxidation.
A maintained strain state accelerates electron and proton transfer during ethanol oxidation.
A maintained strain state improves catalytic activity and selectivity toward CO2.
A maintained strain state increases resistance to catalyst poisoning.
Strain relaxation produces suboptimal intermediate adsorption and reduced catalytic performance.
Optimally annealed strained catalysts should exhibit a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than the unannealed baseline.
Optimally annealed strained catalysts should exhibit a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than the unannealed baseline.
Optimally annealed strained catalysts should produce more CO2 than the unannealed baseline.
The proposed strain-performance relationship applies only when annealing does not cause significant sintering, agglomeration, or other morphological changes.

A statistically indistinguishable onset potential, current density, and product distribution after confirmed strain modification and exclusion of morphology changes would falsify the strain-governed hypothesis.
